lesson_title: The Speedometer Question: Limits and First Principles
hook_text: Your taxi averaged 80 km/h — but what did the speedometer say at THIS exact moment? That question invented calculus.
clip_script: A taxi covers 160 kilometres in two hours. Average speed: eighty. Easy — distance over time. But here's the question that broke mathematics open for three hundred years: what did the speedometer read at one exact instant? An instant has no distance and no time. Zero over zero. Undefined. So build it. Measure the average over one minute around that instant: ninety. Over one second: closer. A tenth of a second: closer still. The shorter the interval, the less the speed can drift inside it — the averages are closing in on ONE number. That number, the limit of average speeds as the interval shrinks to nothing, IS the speedometer reading. Now do it to a curve. Average gradient between two points: rise over run. Slide the second point toward the first and the averages settle — on y equals x squared at x equals one, they read three, two comma five, two comma one, two comma nought one... landing on two. That landing is called the derivative, and the recipe behind it — first principles — is where every rule of calculus is born.
visual_style: A minibus dash with a speedometer needle, a stopwatch interval visibly shrinking around one instant, then a glowing parabola with a secant line pivoting into a tangent as averages tick down to 2.
mood: Curious, cinematic, the thrill of an old riddle cracking.
pacing: Rolling start, tightening rhythm as the interval shrinks, a satisfied stop when the tangent locks in.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and build the machine that reads change at a single instant.
